blocks.text: 1. Replication
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447163258-656811885.png
Replication is the complementary strategy to sharding. Where sharding splits data across machines, replication keeps copies of it to improve availability and reliability.
It works by maintaining multiple identical copies of the same data across separate machines, a strategy aimed squarely at resilience and read scalability.
2. Copying Not Splitting
Sharding splits different data across machines; replication instead copies the same data onto multiple machines.
Each replica holds a complete, identical copy of the data it replicates rather than a partial slice of it.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Strategy","What each machine holds"],"rows":[["Sharding","A different slice of the overall data"],["Replication","A complete, identical copy of the same data"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Why A Copy Helps
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447163258-291252838.png
Because every replica holds a full copy of the data, a single machine failing does not take the whole dataset down with it.
A surviving replica keeps serving queries while the failed one is repaired or replaced.
4. Read Scaling Through Replicas
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447163259-500581549.png
Multiple identical replicas can each answer read queries independently and in parallel.
That spreads query load across several machines instead of overloading a single one.
5. Keeping Replicas In Sync
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447163259-407597498.png
A write to one replica needs to eventually reach every other replica too.
That synchronization process is where replication's real complexity lives.
6. Synchronous Versus Asynchronous Replication
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447163259-648377335.png
Synchronous replication waits for every replica to confirm before a write is considered finished; asynchronous replication does not.
That choice trades write speed against guaranteed consistency across replicas.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Replication mode","Tradeoff"],"rows":[["Synchronous","Slower writes, all replicas confirmed consistent"],["Asynchronous","Faster writes, replicas may briefly lag"]]}

blocks.text: 7. Stale Data Window
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447163260-4977918.png
Asynchronous replication opens a brief window where one replica can lag behind another.
A query that happens to hit the lagging replica can momentarily miss the most recent update.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: A document deleted and then immediately re-searched can still appear in results if that particular query happens to hit a replica that has not yet received the deletion under asynchronous replication.

blocks.text: 8. Combining Sharding And Replication
A large system often uses sharding and replication together rather than choosing one over the other.
Each shard gets its own set of replicas, delivering scale and resilience at the same time.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: A production vector database often shards data across many machines for scale, then replicates each individual shard for resilience, combining both strategies.

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing When Replication Is Worth The Added Complexity

blocks.alt: Recognizing When Replication Is Worth The Added Complexity
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447163260-530849592.png
Production systems that need high availability need replication.
Early prototypes with no uptime requirement can skip replication initially.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Confusing replication, which copies the same data, with sharding, which splits different data.
Assuming asynchronous replication guarantees every replica is always perfectly up to date.
Choosing synchronous replication everywhere without considering its write latency cost.
Skipping replication entirely for a production system that needs high availability.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Replication keeps multiple identical copies of the same data across separate machines.
Sharding splits different data across machines; replication instead copies the same data.
A surviving replica keeps serving queries while a failed one gets repaired.
Multiple replicas can each answer read queries independently, spreading query load.
Keeping replicas synchronized after every write is where replication's real complexity lives.
Synchronous replication guarantees consistency at the cost of write speed; asynchronous trades the reverse.
Asynchronous replication opens a brief window where a replica can lag behind and return stale data.
Large systems often combine sharding and replication together for both scale and resilience.
